dek: A Las Vegas handicapper and author whose first betting book came out from Harper & Row in 1974. On 20 Nov 2026 none of his sales sites worked, and the last archived copy of his sales page is from February 2023. Buyer posts we found, from 2009 to 2022, are mostly negative, with a few positive voices.

short_answer: Kelso Sturgeon is a real, long running name in pick selling and betting books. The Internet Archive holds his Guide to Sports Betting, published by Harper & Row in New York in 1974, and Google Books lists The Complete Guide to Football Betting he wrote with Jim Feist in 1997. His bio on Don Best and on an archived Vegas Sports Masters page gives a long list of further credentials, a Las Vegas home and a phone number. In that sense he is a real seller, not an invented persona.

On 20 Nov 2026 we could not find a working place to buy his picks. The Vegas Sports Masters site he sold through no longer loads, the Wayback Machine has no copy of his page newer than 7 Feb 2023, its .com domain goes to a parking page, and the old kelsosportshandicapping.com address showed unrelated content in a 2026 archive copy. A Swedish betting blog sits on kelsosturgeon.com; we saw nothing linking it to him.

We found no full record of his picks. Buyer posts on HandicappingReviews.org and Pregame.com from 2009 to 2022 lean clearly negative, with repeated complaints about losing runs, very large unit plays, upsell calls and refunds, and a few buyers who said he won for them. The archived refund policy matches those complaints: no refunds once picks are delivered. Treat any current offer under his name with care and ask for a complete record first.
pricing_intro: We found no live seller price on 20 Nov 2026. The archived Vegas Sports Masters shop page from Dec 2022 showed no products in the copy we opened, and the sales page itself told buyers to call or text for daily wagers. The only prices we saw are on an undated third party review, so treat them as history, not a current offer.
pricing: Third party listing, undated; not a verified current offer
About $200 to $300 per sport per season
"call or text me at 1-702-420-5074 or 1-646-526-2559 for daily wagers"
guarantee: The Vegas Sports Masters privacy and refund policy, in a Wayback Machine copy from 26 Mar 2023, says that for "Pay After You Win" services "there can be no refunds," and that for "Pay-First" services "once you, the customer, have been linked to any selection pages, received selections via e-mail or received selections by telephone, no refund can be issued. We will, however, provide an alternative service if you, the customer, are dissatisfied." It adds that a guarantee of free service "will not entitle that customer to a money back refund" and that picks "will not, as a rule, be guaranteed." Only printed publications carried a 30 day return for refund or exchange.

Buyers describe the same pattern. One wrote in 2016 that the service sent him the wrong games, admitted the mistake and offered only extra games. Another wrote in 2019 that he asked for a refund and got no reply, and a 2011 forum member described a dispute over a refund he said he was owed. These are single, unverified accounts, but they fit the written policy: credits or replacement picks, not money back.

claims_note: The career claims are the strongest part of his pitch, and the ones we could check hold up: the 1974 Harper & Row book exists, and so does the 1997 football book with Jim Feist. A long career in betting media does not show that his picks beat the closing line or the vig.

The banner wins are picked by the seller. Forum members wrote in 2011, and a reviewer wrote in 2016, that he promoted winning big unit plays and said little about losing ones. That is one reading of his marketing, not a measured fact.

The unit sizes are very large. A 2019 buyer posted three days of his NCAA tournament cards: we add them to 165, 150 and 170 units, made of one 50 or 100 unit play plus a 25 unit play and several 15 unit plays each day. At that scale one losing 100 unit play costs as much as about seven 15 unit winners pay at -110, so a record in wins and losses says little without the units.
record: What a buyer can verify independently: nothing that we could find. We found no full, time stamped log of every Kelso Sturgeon pick, no contest results under his name, and no court or regulator record about the service. His Don Best page shows a bio but no record or dated picks.

What the seller published: banner results such as a 100 unit Falcons win and a Monday night sweep on the archived 2023 page. A 2009 Pregame thread also quotes an 11 and 0 run on his top college basketball plays. These are chosen runs, not a record.

Buyers posted their own partial results. A 2019 buyer posted a full March Madness card that he said went 0 and 7 on one day, a 2017 reviewer listed eight college basketball losses in a row, and a 2016 buyer said he quit a November football package at 3 and 5. A 2014 buyer said he broke even over two weeks. These are partial and unverified.

customers_intro: Independent buyer evidence on Kelso Sturgeon is mostly on one review site and two forum threads, and none of it is newer than 2022. Below is everything we found and how much weight it can carry.

customers.text: We read 13 buyer comments on HandicappingReviews.org dated 2013 to 2022, two Pregame forum threads from 2009, 2011 and 2019, and a 2007 TheRX thread. Ten of the 13 review site comments are negative, one is mixed, one neutral and one positive. The same complaints repeat across nine years and two sites: long losing runs, very large unit plays that lost, constant calls to upgrade, wins promoted while losses went unmentioned, and refunds that did not come. One 2019 complaint appears on both sites with the same pick list, so it is likely one buyer. On the positive side, a 2013 buyer said he did his homework and won for him, a 2014 buyer broke even in two weeks, a 2011 forum member called him a long term winner, and a 2016 reviewer said he made money years earlier but not lately. That is a consistent pattern over many years, but every account is unverified and we found nothing newer than 2022. Our Reddit check found only a 2017 question about his book with Jim Feist, with no buyer reports; the Arctic Shift full text search timed out for most queries on 20 Nov 2026.
A reviewer on HandicappingReviews.org wrote that the picks cost him a lot of money before he decided they were a waste of time, and that only the seller was making money.

A Pregame member posted the college basketball card he bought for the NCAA tournament and said it went 0 for 7 on Saturday after losing 55 units on Friday. He said he asked for a refund and got no reply. The same pick list was posted as a review on HandicappingReviews.org the next day. Other members replied that he had been selling picks for decades and told the buyer to stop.

A reviewer said he lost eight college basketball games over three days of the 2017 tournament and listed the teams. Two more 2017 reviews on the same page, from June and September, called the picks very poor without giving results.

A buyer of a November football package said he quit after starting 3 and 5. He wrote that he was once sent the wrong games, that the service admitted the error later, and that it offered only extra games, not money. He added that even the right games would have left him at 6 and 5, which he said would still have lost money.

A reviewer said the picks made him money a few years earlier but had been disappointing since. He complained that "he never shows his losses" on the website and that 50, 100 and 200 unit plays were sold as near locks.
A family wrote that the service kept mailing promotions to a relative who had died almost a year earlier and that they could not reach anyone to stop it. This is about marketing, not picks.
A reviewer said he is not a good college handicapper and is wrong a lot, and told readers to go elsewhere. No results were given.
A buyer said the service kept pushing upgrades before his current package had run out and that he would not sign up again.
A buyer two weeks into a package said he had broken even both weeks and that the site and service were decent.
A reviewer said he bought one month of basketball a few seasons earlier and that the late season picks were no better than a coin flip. He used harsher words; this is his opinion.
A reviewer said the picks can look unusual, often underdogs, but that the handicapper does his homework and had led him to wins.

A Pregame member wrote that he used the NFL, NBA and baseball picks for over a year and lost thousands of dollars. He alleged constant sales calls and a dispute over a refund he said he was owed. We could not verify any of it.
In the same thread another member defended him as a long term winner, said every capper has losing streaks, and said he used to get useful free mailers from him.

A third member advised following him only on hot streaks and bigger plays, and said he talked about winners while skipping losers, citing two big unit losses in one week of which only one was mentioned.

A TheRX member reposted a Las Vegas Sporting News column listing ten touts to avoid. Sturgeon's name appears only in a closing list of further names, with no specific claim about him. It is an old opinion piece, not a buyer report.

A Better Business Bureau search for Kelso Sturgeon in Las Vegas returned no results. On Reddit, the only post naming him we found was a 2017 question about a betting book he co wrote with Jim Feist, with no buyer reports. Our web searches found no Sportsbook Review or Covers thread with buyer results, and no news report of legal action.

conflicts: Several web addresses tied to his name no longer belong to his business as far as we can tell. kelsosturgeon.com is a Swedish betting and casino blog, kelsosportshandicapping.com showed unrelated content in an April 2026 archive copy, and vegassportsmasters.com sent us to a domain parking page. A buyer should not assume any of these speak for him.

The archived Vegas Sports Masters page also sold picks from other handicappers, including Jim Feist, Jim Hurley, Hollis Barnhart and Noel Michaels, so it was a storefront for several names, not his alone. His 1997 football book was co written with Jim Feist.

A competing pick site, Sports Information Traders, has an undated page about him that says auto dialer calls offering a "game of the night" came from a number it links to his service, and that a web search tied the same number to Wayne Root. It is a rival seller's page, gives no dates or evidence, and says its own team never used his picks, so we give it little weight.
strengths: A real, named person with a long public career, two betting books we could confirm (1974 and 1997), and a Las Vegas phone number on his old sales page.
His bio is detailed and specific, which makes the career claims checkable in principle.
The old storefront published a written refund policy, so buyers could see the terms before paying.
Some buyers over the years said he won for them, broke even, or did real homework.
concerns: No working sales site, prices or terms from the seller on 20 Nov 2026; the last archived copy of his sales page is from February 2023.
No full public record. Every result we saw was chosen by the seller or posted by a single buyer.
Buyer posts from 2011 to 2022 repeat the same complaints: losing runs, upsell calls and refunds not paid.
Very large unit plays, from 15 to 100 units on one card, so one loss can erase many winners.
Old domains under his name now show unrelated sites, which makes it easy to confuse a copycat with the real service.
checklist: Ask for every pick from the last 12 months with the line, the odds, the units and the time it was sent. A list of hot runs is not a record.
Confirm you are dealing with the real seller. Several old domains under his name now show other content.
Get refund or guarantee terms in writing before you pay. The last policy we found offered replacement picks, not cash.
Count units, not wins. A 100 unit loss can wipe out many 15 unit winners.
Say no to upgrades until your current package has ended and you have graded it.
Write down each pick yourself the moment you receive it, with the line you can actually get.
faq: He is a real person with a long career in betting media and pick selling, including a 1974 Harper & Row betting book we could confirm, and his old sales page gave a Las Vegas phone number. We could not verify that his picks win over time, we found no working sales site on 20 Nov 2026, and buyer posts from 2009 to 2022 are mostly negative. We found no court or regulator action involving him.
How much does Kelso Sturgeon cost?

We found no current price from the seller. An undated third party review lists daily picks at $25 to $75 and a monthly package at $499, and the archived 2023 page asked buyers to call or text for daily wagers.
Does Kelso Sturgeon have a verified record?
No. His old sales page showed selected wins such as a 100 unit game of the year. We found no independent, time stamped log of every pick.

The last refund policy we found, archived in March 2023, says no refunds once you have received picks, with an alternative service offered if you are dissatisfied, and that a guarantee only entitles you to free service, not money back.
Is Kelso Sturgeon still selling picks?

His Don Best profile is still online, but on 20 Nov 2026 the Vegas Sports Masters site he sold through did not load, the newest archive copy of his page is from February 2023, and its .com domain went to a parking page. The newest buyer review we found is from 2022.

We cannot tell you he wins, because nobody has published a full record. What we can see is a long run of buyer complaints, very large unit sizes and no cash refunds. If you find a current offer under his name, confirm it is really him and ask for a complete record first.
